extracted.intended_audience: scholars and graduate students in philosophy of mathematics and mathematical practice; mathematicians interested in the epistemology and methodology of proofs, diagrams, notation, and mathematical design
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts criteria and desiderata philosophers and mathematicians use to evaluate proofs, visual representations, notations, explanations, value judgments, and design choices in mathematical practice. Focuses on conceptual standards (e.g., purity, beauty, modularity) and methodological prescriptions (e.g., controlled use of diagrams, notation trade-offs).

rubrics_metrics.name: Role and types of visual representations
rubrics_metrics.description: Visual representations encompass internal visual imagery/imagination and external representations—diagrams, symbolic systems, notations, computer images, etc.—and are widespread in past and contemporary mathematical practices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize both discovery and justificatory/epistemic roles for visual representations; treat internal and external representations as distinct kinds with varied functions across domains and contexts (Giaquinto, Brown, collected literature).

rubrics_metrics.name: Pictures/diagrams can function as proofs (picture-proofs)
rubrics_metrics.description: Pictures (or 'picture-proofs') can sometimes prove mathematical propositions and serve as instruments to perceive mathematical structure (Brown's claim that 'pictures' can prove propositions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be open to non-linguistic argument forms; examine carefully whether the picture contains sufficient structure/constraints to count as a legitimate proof rather than mere intuition or heuristic. See Brown's examples ranging from intermediate value theorem to propositions about natural numbers and series.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methodology: case studies for studying visual representations
rubrics_metrics.description: The dominant empirical/analytic method for investigating visual representations is detailed case studies of specific proofs, diagrams, or practices (e.g., Manders on Euclid, Carter on free probability, Starikova on Cayley graphs).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use fine-grained analysis of particular examples to test conceptual accounts and to reveal domain-specific visual operations; beware of overgeneralizing from single cases without taxonomy of visual kinds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manders' distinction: co-exact vs exact diagram attributes
rubrics_metrics.description: Co-exact attributes are insensitive to a range of continuous deformations of a concrete diagram (e.g., two circles intersect); exact attributes are sensitive and obtain only in isolated cases (e.g., tangency, exact equality of lengths). Manders argues Euclid's diagram-based attributions are limited to co-exact attributes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating diagram-based inferences, check whether the attributed feature is co-exact (thus reliably 'read off' the diagram) or exact (must be established by prior textual/deductive claims); controlled use of diagrams is defensible if restricted to co-exact attributions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diagrams as sources of discovery and proof-structuring
rubrics_metrics.description: Diagrams can inspire definitions and proof strategies, serve as frameworks for parts of a proof, and help break complex proofs into manageable components (Carter, Starikova, De Toffoli & Giardino examples).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess visual representations for their heuristic/creative functions (discovery, concept formation) as well as their justificatory roles; document how diagrams guide the selection of definitions, lemmas, or decomposition of proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manipulative imagination and epistemic actions
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners acquire via training a manipulable imagination that permits them to perform epistemic actions (Kirsh & Maglio) on visual representations, which plays a substantial epistemic role in proving and discovery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether a representation affords manipulable operations (transformations, thought-experiments) that reliably yield insights or proof steps; consider the role of training and communal practices in making such manipulations reliable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Good notation benefits (economy, generalization, computation, explanation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Good mathematical notations enable economical mathematical expressions, promote generalizations and new developments, provide computational power, and enable mathematical explanation and understanding (Colyvan; Macbeth: notations can embody reasoning).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing or designing notation, examine whether it makes expressions concise, highlights general patterns, facilitates computations, and helps convey/expose conceptual relations—not merely serves as shorthand.

rubrics_metrics.name: Notations as constitutive and cognitive supports
rubrics_metrics.description: External symbolic systems may be constitutive of the mathematical concepts they represent and play a central cognitive role by supporting mathematical operations (De Cruz & De Smedt, Dutilh Novaes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider whether a notation merely records pre-existing concepts or actively shapes concept formation and cognitive procedures; evaluate its role in acquisition and historical development of mathematical abilities.

rubrics_metrics.name: De Toffoli's notation-evaluation criteria: expressiveness, calculability, transparency
rubrics_metrics.description: Three evaluative dimensions for notation: expressiveness (information captured), calculability (what calculations the notation allows), and transparency (how intuitive/natural the notation is to use).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acknowledge trade-offs between criteria (e.g., Euler vs Venn diagrams). No algorithmic ranking is provided; context and goals determine priorities. If two notations tie on two criteria, prefer the one that does better on the third.

rubrics_metrics.name: Steiner's account of explanatory proofs: characterizing property and generalizability
rubrics_metrics.description: An explanatory proof depends on a 'characterizing property' of something mentioned in the theorem and should be generalizable so that changing the property shows how the proof and theorem change (Steiner 1978).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate explanatory status by checking whether the proof leverages a property that characterizes relevant structure and whether the proof's dependence on that property yields understanding through generalization. Note documented counterexamples and critiques.

rubrics_metrics.name: Kitcher's unification account of explanation (explanatory store)
rubrics_metrics.description: A proof is explanatory if it belongs to a theory's 'explanatory store'; unification is measured by minimizing the number of genuine derivation patterns while maximizing the number of theorems proven (Kitcher 1989).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess explanatory power in terms of unification across theorems and derivation schemes, but be mindful of counterexamples where brute-force or algorithmic proofs may score highly on unification yet fail to be intuitively explanatory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understanding as possession of mathematical abilities
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematical understanding can be conceived in terms of an agent's possession of certain mathematical abilities (Avigad); accounting for understanding in a case amounts to characterizing the relevant abilities (e.g., abilities to manipulate, represent, apply lemmas).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging whether a proof or presentation conveys understanding, specify which abilities it fosters (e.g., problem-solving moves, recognition of patterns) rather than relying solely on subjective impressions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proofs must be content-sensitive (beyond formal proofs) to convey understanding
rubrics_metrics.description: To explain how one reasons mathematically on the basis of content, we need a notion of proof different from bare formal proofs—proofs that expose content and reasoning routes convey understanding (Macbeth; Folina family-resemblance approach).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether a proof presentation makes mathematical content and key reasoning steps visible (interfaces, encapsulated lemmas) rather than hiding everything inside intractable formal derivations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beauty / Enlightenment as evaluative criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: When mathematicians call a result 'beautiful' they often mean it is enlightening (Rota)—involves grasping the role, relevance, and relations of a statement; Cellucci: beauty consists in yielding understanding by showing how parts fit (grasp of fit).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate beauty by its capacity to produce understanding/enlightenment: does the proof expose relations, fit of parts, and the theorem's role in a broader structure? Use case studies (e.g., Euler's identity, Meno square example).

rubrics_metrics.name: Topical purity
rubrics_metrics.description: A solution is topically pure when it uses only the mathematical resources (axioms, definitions, inferences) that determine the topic of the problem; impure solutions employ resources outside the topic (Detlefsen & Arana).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check which background resources a proof or solution invokes; pure solutions are epistemically stable (retracting parts dissolves the problem), whereas impure ones may rely on removable external resources (Furstenberg's topology-based proof of infinitude of primes is impure).

rubrics_metrics.name: Fruitfulness of calculi/systems
rubrics_metrics.description: A calculus is fruitful if it 'corresponds to the innermost nature of frequent wants'—i.e., supplies lemmas/theorems that are repeatedly useful so practitioners can avoid re-deriving routine results and can solve problems more mechanically/systematically (Yap interpreting Gauss).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether adopting a system reduces repetitive derivations, supplies reusable tools, enables systematic decomposition of problems, and integrates well with existing methods (example: congruence theory makes many proofs shorter and cleaner).

rubrics_metrics.name: Other evaluative values (depth, fit, interestingness, motivation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Philosophers consider a range of additional value judgments applied to mathematics such as depth, fit, interestingness, and whether proofs are well-motivated (Arana; Raman-Sundström & Öhman; Thomas; Morris).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include these dimensions when evaluating mathematical work; they are distinct from correctness and may interact with explanation, beauty, purity, and fruitfulness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematical design: modularity, interfaces, and encapsulation
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematics should be designed to have a modular structure (Avigad): definitions and lemmas act as modules/interfaces that hide nitty-gritty details (encapsulation) and allow components to be reused or ignored when not relevant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate mathematical organization by its modularity: does the structure aid understanding, isolate errors, support concurrent work, and enable reuse? Use the software-engineering analogy to check for clear interfaces and appropriate hiding of implementation details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design benefits checklist (understandability, error-finding, concurrency, reuse)
rubrics_metrics.description: Modularity and good design in mathematics bring benefits: (i) easier to understand; (ii) easier to find problems or mistakes; (iii) allows different agents to work on parts concurrently; (iv) allows components to be reused in different contexts (Avigad).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging exposition or the structuring of a theory, check whether these practical benefits obtain; prefer structures that maximize these benefits in the relevant context.
